title: Screen Coverage EDA
lead: How defenses guard ball screens in the ten tracked games. What each coverage looks like, when it shows, who is in the screen, what comes before it, and why switches are hard to read.

items: **Two labels per screen.** bhrDefType is the ball handler's defender (over, under, switch, ice or blitz). scrDefType is the screener's defender (drop, show, switch, ice, blitz or none). SkillCorner's raw label for drop is soft, and I call it drop throughout
**One coverage per screen.** Switch, ice and blitz always come as a pair. Over or under always pairs with drop, show or none. So the two labels make one coverage with seven values
**Five main coverages.** Over · drop, over · show (hedge), under · drop, under · show and switch. I left ice and blitz out of the model

blocks.text: Are the Ten Games Typical?

The season files count direct ball screens only (the handler or screener shot, passed for an assist or drew a foul right after the screen). They give each defender's coverage across the league, never the pair together.

blocks.title: Handler's defender: ten games vs season
Screener's defender: ten games vs season

items: **Over is the default.** Over · drop and over · show make up 66% of screens. Guessing the more common one is right 33% of the time
**The sample matches the season.** Season direct ball screens are 66% over, 15% under and 18% switch. Only 2 of 22,085 have no coverage on the handler's defender, and 89 none on the screener's
**Ice and blitz are rare everywhere.** Ice is 1.0% of season direct ball screens and blitz 0.3%

blocks.text: The four players of the screen from 3 s before to 2 s after the pick frame. Lines are averages. A chart about one defender splits by his own coverage, so the handler's defender shows over, under and switch and the screener's defender shows drop, show and switch. I left out ice and blitz. The dashed line is the pick frame, the same moment as the play viewer's Pick line.

items: **Time 0 is the pick frame** (picks.frame). The handler comes off the screener's shoulder a median 0.2 s later (middle half 0.2 to 0.4 s)

**Level vs the screen** is a player's distance from the hoop minus the screen spot's, in feet. Above the screen is positive and below is negative. Over keeps the handler's defender above the screen and under takes him below it. Show brings the screener's defender up to the ball and drop keeps him back
**Who is who.** ballhandlerDefId and screenerDefId name the defenders before any switch. The matchups table agrees on 95% of screens just before the screen

items: **Under goes below the screen.** The handler's defender is 3.1 ft below the screen level 0.4 s after the pick frame. Going over he is 1.6 ft above it
**Show meets the ball.** The screener's defender is 7.2 ft from the handler 0.4 s after the pick frame. Drop keeps him 10.2 ft away
**Switches trade assignments late.** By +2 s the handler's own defender is 14.0 ft away and the screener's defender 5.5 ft
**Under starts with a high handler.** 1 s before the pick frame the handler is 10.1 ft above the screen when his defender goes under and 8.5 ft when he goes over
**The matchups table agrees on switches.** 71% of switches hand the handler to the screener's defender 1.5 s after the screen, against 5% of over and under screens
Averages hide spread. Single screens overlap a lot, which the next section measures

blocks.text: If two coverages only look different after the screen, a model that sees those frames is recognising the coverage. Before the screen it has to predict it.

items: **Separation (AUC).** Take one screen of each kind at random. The AUC is how often a measure puts them the right way round. 0.5 is a coin flip and 1 is always right. Each point is one measure at one moment
The charts follow each measure from −3 s to +2 s for the three questions a model faces

items: **Under or over shows late.** Best AUC 0.59 1 s before the pick frame and 0.97 0.4 s after it
**Show or drop shows first.** The screener's defender's level separates 0.67 at −0.4 s and 0.84 at the pick frame
**Switch shows last.** Best 0.64 at the pick frame, 0.85 at +1 s and 0.91 at +2 s
**So a read before the screen leans on set-up and context.** A model allowed to look 0.5 to 1 s past the screen is mostly reading a coverage already visible in the tracking
One measure at one moment is a floor. Combining measures and frames separates better, most of all before the screen
SkillCorner's labels come from its own tracking model, so part of the after-screen separation is the labelling rule itself

items: **Switches grow as the shot clock runs down.** 7% of screens with 18+ s left, 25% with 6 s or less
**Under follows how high the handler starts.** 32% go under when he is 13+ ft above the screen 1 s before, 22% when he is within 3 ft
**Location type barely matters.** The under rate only moves from 17% to 23%

blocks.text: Coverage by the size of the four players. I grouped each player's archetype into guard, wing or big, using the archetypes exactly as the Archetypes tab fits them.
Guard, Wing or Big

items: **Guard.** Primary Ball Handler, Secondary Ball Handler and Slasher
**Wing.** Off Screen Shooter, Movement Shooter, Stationary Shooter and Athletic Finisher
**Big.** Post Scorer, Roll & Cut Big and Versatile Big

**Offense sets the group.** A player's offensive archetype sets his group, and all of the 200 players in these screens have one. The defensive archetypes are a check (Chaser counts as guard). 47 of 49 Anchor Bigs are offensive bigs, and 26 of 46 Chasers are offensive guards

blocks.text: Would Archetypes Leak Into the Model?

items: **No coverage label goes in.** No coverage share enters the clusters, so an archetype never holds the answer directly

**A small side door through matchups.** 9 defensive clustering features use who he was assigned to guard (the matchups table). After a switch a big is assigned to a guard, so a big who switches a lot drifts toward guard-like values

**The graded game is inside the fit.** The archetypes were fitted on all ten games and on season files that include them (and later games). A model graded on a held-out game would use groups shaped partly by that game

**Safest form.** The guard, wing or big group from the offensive archetype. It rests on how a player scores and moves on offense, the furthest from coverage. For zero leakage, refit the archetypes without the graded game in each fold
**Fair for a coach's question.** A scout knows who is a guard, a wing or a big before tip-off. Position is a fair input as long as it comes from data outside the graded game

blocks.text: Ways to Read Switches Better

items: **Give it the possession's memory.** Cross-matched now, an earlier switch, an earlier ball screen. The 1.6 s window cannot see them, and they are now the largest signals left

**Keep the players' size.** Since 2026-11-19 the switch decision reads guard, wing or big for the four screen players, taken from data outside the graded game. It closed most of the size gap in the table above
**Give it who guards whom right now.** The current matchups assignment of the four players, read only up to the moment of prediction

**Lower the bar for switch.** Over · show and over · drop win most close frames. A switch threshold, or dividing each coverage's probability by its share, catches more switches at some cost in false alarms
**Check switches with no hand-over in the play viewer.** 55 labelled switches never hand the handler over in the matchups table by +3 s

items: **Geometry adds nothing measurable to the five main coverages.** From −1 s to +0.4 s the change in log loss stays between −0.003 and +0.010. Every interval clear of zero is a small loss (geometry at −1 s)
**Single measures stay near a coin flip.** Separations sit near 0.5 to 0.6 and the best is 0.62. The defenders' own levels and distances already carry what the geometry implies

**Time to act and the shot clock score the same** (differences of 0.0002). They only differ in the last seconds of a period. I used time to act in the models because it is the clock the offense actually faces
**Geometry matters for ice**, the one coverage it describes well
These measures enter a linear model here. A transformer sees the same positions directly

blocks.text: Simple Baselines

items: **How they work.** Each baseline predicts a screen's coverage from the shares in a reference group, with one screen of each coverage added so nothing gets probability zero, and the league mix added with the weight of five screens
**No peeking.** Groups built from games leave out the screen's own game. 'Earlier coverages' and 'previous coverage' use only screens before this one in the same game
**Season baseline.** The handler's season share of over, under, switch, ice and blitz times the screener's season share of show and drop, each pulled toward the league with the weight of 20 screens

**Scores.** Accuracy is how often the most likely coverage was right. Log loss is the average of minus the log of the probability given to the true coverage. Lower is better, and guessing all seven equally scores 1.95

items: **The bar from league shares alone is 1.52.** Its accuracy is only 26% because over · drop and over · show are nearly tied, so which one it screens flips from game to game
**Context alone says little.** No honest look-up moves log loss by more than 0.02 (best is 'By shot-clock band' at 1.50)
**A team's game plan is worth at most 1.42.** That is the score with the defense's whole-game mix, which includes the answer
**So the signal has to come from the tracking around the screen** (When It Shows)
**Ice (14) and blitz (4) cannot be learned from 1,514 screens.** I left them out of the model

sections.title: What This Means for the Model

items: **Label.** Five coverages. Ice (14) and blitz (4) are too rare to learn
**Timing.** Show or drop reads before the screen. Under or over and switch mostly show after it, so a read before the screen leans on set-up and context

**Switches are the gap.** The size of the screener's defender, a cross-match and an earlier switch all move the switch rate. The live model has read size since 2026-11-19 but still misses the possession's history (Reading Switches)
**Personnel needs care.** Guard, wing or big is fair for a coach's question, but it should come from data outside the graded game (Who Is in the Screen)
**Never inputs.** bhrOutcomes, scrOutcomes, direct, and anything about the shot or points. All are recorded after the coverage
**Size.** 1,514 labelled screens, about 151 per game, with most defenses seen in one game only. Split by game and report each held-out game
